Axios AM
By Mike Allen · Nov 04, 2026

🌊 Good Wednesday morning — and welcome to the post-election world.

  • Smart Brevity™ count: 2,394 words ... 9 mins. Thanks to Noah Bressner for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

🚨 AP call at 11:36 p.m. ET: WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats have won the US Senate, ending Republican dominance in Washington by harnessing voters' frustration with Trump.

  • At 1:24 a.m.: Democrats win the US House and take unified control of Congress as voters deliver resounding rebuke to Trump.

🗳️ Nail-biter in Mississippi: Democrat Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) by 43 votes with an estimated 96% of ballots counted. Full election results.
 
 
1 big thing: The Trump obliteration
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

Make no mistake: Democrats won by epic, sometimes historic margins across red and blue states, up and down ballots, obliterating almost everything President Trump, and a Republican Party remade wholly in his image, built over the past decade in American politics, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen write in a "Behind the Curtain" column.

  • Why it matters: Trump and Republicans are left with a mostly white, mostly old House and Senate minority, confronting a younger, more diverse ascendant Democratic Party with power and margins it hasn't held in 18 years, since the dawn of the Obama era.

📊 The results speak louder than any words we can write:

  • Democrats won Senate races in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio, and perhaps Mississippi en route to what could be a 55-seat majority.
  • Democrats won swing districts all across red America, with national average margins of victory of roughly 13 points, according to a New York Times estimate. Dems appear headed for a 250+-seat majority, an 18-year high.
  • Texas is now a Democratic state, top to bottom — unthinkable mere months ago. James Talarico crushed Ken Paxton (55% to 43%) like it was Connecticut. State Representative Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 32 years.
  • Pastor Adam Hamilton is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years.
  • North Carolina looks like a true-blue state after Democrats flipped the Senate seat and likely ousted Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) — meaning he led the GOP drive to keep the House.
  • North Carolina's congressional delegation could swing from 10R-4D to 5R-9D. Georgia was even worse for Republicans, where they lost all power at the state and U.S. Senate levels.
  • Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) predicted on X that the losses were so widespread, so deep, so severe that Republicans might not "have a shot at Senate control until 2032."

💡 How to think about last night more broadly: This is a 50-50 nation with fast, whiplash shifts in power at the federal level due to persistent discontent with the party in power. So, on one hand, this isn't terribly surprising.

  • On the other, Republican losses were so deep, so wide, so everywhere that it would be foolish to see this as anything but a massive repudiation of Trump, his agenda, his style, his rhetoric and his presidency.

If anything, what's left of the Republican Party is more pro-Trump and less likely to challenge him. His critics, even the timid ones, were ousted long before the general election. So Republicans are left with two more years of riding a very unpopular leader managing a very unpopular war. A trapped, embarrassed Trump is even more unpredictable.

  • Democrats have the numbers to investigate Trump, his family and supporters, and the power to set the agenda in the House and Senate.

The bottom line: Voters nationally said government corruption was a "crucial issue" in their vote for Congress. Democrats will spend months trying to rehab a party that, despite its victory, remains deeply unpopular as a brand. Expect a vigorous fight between Mamdani-like socialists and Schumer-like center-leftists.

 
 
2. 🌊 Blue tsunami breaks MAGA
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

The 2026 midterms will go down as one of the most sweeping repudiations of a sitting president in modern American history, on a scale reminiscent of the post-Watergate reckoning of 1974, Axios' Zachary Basu writes.

  • Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress, on course to hold at least 54 Senate seats and potentially more than 255 in the House.
  • The wave swept deep into Republican territory, from Texas and Georgia to both Carolinas, flipping hundreds of legislative seats and delivering Democratic trifectas in the unlikeliest of states.
  • Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly contested Senate race and will be the nation's first Muslim senator.
Cover: The New York Post

Takeaways:

1. Texas turns blue: Democrats finally conquered the nation's most coveted Republican stronghold — in a landslide so sweeping that even three-term Gov. Greg Abbott was driven from office.

  • Gina Hinojosa became the state's first Latina governor, while James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton to become the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988.
  • The Democratic onslaught extended across statewide offices and into the legislature after 32 years of GOP dominance.

2. Democrats storm Senate: What once looked like an impossibly difficult map for Democrats gave way to a historic rout, as Republicans watched their 53-seat majority crumble in states Trump carried by double digits.

  • Democrats broke a 94-year losing streak in Kansas, ousted Republicans in Ohio, Iowa and North Carolina, and captured South Carolina for the first time since 1998.
  • In Maine, Democrats finally toppled five-term Sen. Susan Collins after many failed attempts.

3. MAGA coalition collapses: The multiracial, working-class coalition that powered Trump's 2024 comeback fractured spectacularly.

  • AP's nationwide voter survey found roughly 70% of voters under 30 and 60% of Hispanic voters backed Democratic House candidates, amid widespread anger over the economy and the Iran war.

4. GOP House firewall crumbles: Democrats are on course for their largest House majority since 2009.

  • Casualties spanned the entire GOP conference, from MAGA firebrands to battle-tested moderates. Even seats redrawn to shield Republicans from a blue wave fell to Democrats, turning Trump's redistricting offensive into a spectacular miscalculation.
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) arrives to deliver a victory speech at an election night party in Atlanta. Photo: Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images

5. 2028's winners and losers: Yesterday's landslide elevated a new generation of Democratic contenders and cast a shadow over Vice President Vance's presidential ambitions.

  • Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, whose race was called 15 minutes after polls closed, immediately vaulted into the top tier of Democratic prospects. Keisha Lance Bottoms' historic victory for governor removed a key obstacle for both Ossoff and Sen. Raphael Warnock: She could appoint a Democrat to fill their seat if either became president.
  • Vance, Trump's presumed political heir, now faces the fallout from a deeply unpopular Iran war and the collapse of a once-in-a-generation coalition he hoped would carry him to the White House.

3. 🥊 Susie Wiles: Foot on gas
 

Via Truth Social
 

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles made these remarks to senior staff gathered in her office last night, a person in the room tells me:

"We're going to take a page out of President Trump's playbook and keep fighting for the American people. We will not stand by while radical Democrats try to undo the progress we've made by reopening our borders, making our communities less safe, and raising taxes on hardworking families. Anyone who thinks President Trump or this team is going to take our foot off the gas over the next two years is sorely mistaken. We know exactly what's at stake, we know what we're fighting for, and we have no intention of backing down. There is work left to do, and we intend to finish the job."
Via Truth Social

📱President Trump told The New York Times in a phone interview shortly before 10:30 p.m. ET that he's "absolutely willing" to accept the results, and is prepared to work with Democrats:

  • "We'll, you know, look forward to working with them ... We'll probably work something out."
  • He called his decision to go to war with Iran a "very wise decision."

On Republican Darline Graham's stunning loss of her Senate race in South Carolina, Trump said: "I'm just looking at these results as I'm talking ... I see that Darline lost. Wow, that's amazing."

  • Referring to Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, Trump added: "How do you think Lindsey would have done if he ran?"

4. 🤯 Biggest election shockers
 
Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) visit a Whataburger in Austin after winning last night. Photo: James Talarico via X

Democrats racked up stunning margins in red states that President Trump carried in landslides just two years ago, Axios' Hans Nichols writes:

1. The Texas trifecta: Democrats won the races for governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general, giving the party unified control of state government for the first time since 1995.

2. North Carolina was a bloodbath. The man in charge of steering House Republicans to victory — Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee — lost his own seat.

  • He'll join the ranks of other defeated party leaders who spent so much time trying to build a majority that they failed to protect themselves.

3. Hispanic voters swung back. Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in the Rio Grande Valley that President Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close.

  • Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) was leading Republican Tano Tijerina, 66% to 30%.
  • Democrat Bobby Pulido was leading Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, 62% to 38%.
  • Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) was leading Republican Eric Flores, 56% to 40%.

5. ⚡ Hakeem's dream majority
 
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) celebrates while watching election night results in Washington last night. Photo: Kenny Holston/The New York Times

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is set to preside over a commanding Democratic majority after his party swept districts President Trump carried by double digits, Axios' Andrew Solender writes.

  • Why it matters: Democrats' landslide win will make it much, much easier for the likely next speaker to secure the gavel without a sweat and ignore the demands of his progressive wing.

It's a major partisan win for Democrats as a whole, but the party's centrist wing is also hailing the result as a much-needed strategic victory over the left.

  • Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.), a leader of the center-left New Democrat Coalition, told Axios in an interview that Jeffries "now has the space to utilize his full talents as speaker."
  • The size of Democrats' victory, Stanton said, "allows him to govern without worrying about being leveraged by anyone."

🔎 Zoom in: Progressives — particularly "The Bloc," a group made up of hard-charging leftists — had hoped to use a small majority to extract concessions from Jeffries.

  • Many of them have declined to commit to supporting Jeffries as speaker and signaled they would use their votes as leverage to force votes on progressive legislation such as Medicare-for-All, defunding ICE and cutting aid to Israel.
  • But the left's strategy is "going to look different from what it would have been with a smaller margin," one incoming House progressive told Axios, noting that "leaders have more flexibility when they have big majorities."

👓 Between the lines: Stanton noted that most of the incoming Democrats who won in purple and red districts were endorsed by the center-left New Dems — one of Jeffries' most reliable power bases in the caucus.

6. 🤖 AI loses everywhere
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom, Axios' Maria Curi writes.

  • Why it matters: The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead-set on winning.

🔬 Zoom in: All told, nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity could face delays, although most political analysts don't see Democrats permanently blocking construction.

  • Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout.
  • She campaigned on keeping a moratorium on data center construction in place until at least mid-2027.
  • The state accounts for 41% of new U.S. capacity expected in 2028, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis.
Via X

Democrats also won gubernatorial races in Ohio, Georgia and Arizona — the three states expected to have the most new data center capacity after Texas. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restricting construction.

  • Out of 41 data center measures on the ballot across 10 states, about two dozen proposals designed to restrict or block development appeared to have passed based on initial returns.

💰 The other side: In California, a measure that would've enacted a 5% wealth tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in assets appeared headed for defeat after facing heavy opposition from Silicon Valley.

7. 🍑 Night of historic firsts
 
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms embraces her daughter Lincoln at an election night party in Atlanta. Photo: Brynn Anderson/AP

Yesterday's elections delivered a string of historic firsts, breaking barriers in governors' mansions and the Senate, Axios' Julianna Bragg writes.

  • With her victory in Georgia, former Atlanta mayor and Biden aide Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the first Black woman governor in U.S. history.
  • Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Crowley were elected the first Black governors in Florida and Wisconsin, respectively.
  • Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) won New Hampshire's open Senate seat, becoming the first openly gay man elected to the chamber.
  • In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim to serve in the Senate.
  • Deb Haaland (D) won New Mexico's governor's race, becoming the first Indigenous woman elected governor of a U.S. state. Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) became the first Indigenous woman elected to the Senate.

More historic firsts.
 
 
8. 🏛️ D.C. elects socialist mayor
 
D.C. mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George votes at Ida B. Wells Middle School in Washington yesterday. Photo: Daniel Heuer/Reuters

D.C.'s next mayor will be democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George, who swept her primary in June amid unhappiness with the city's direction and promises to expand affordable child care, Axios D.C.'s Cuneyt Dil reports.

  • Lewis George's biggest task will be rebuilding the capital's economy, which has lost 45,600 jobs since President Trump returned to office.

🦆 Voters also overwhelmingly voted in favor of banning foie gras, a ballot initiative that invited fury from chefs like José Andrés and the owner of Butterworth's, a Capitol Hill French bistro popular among Trump's circle.

10. 🏈 1 fun thing: College football reveal
 
College Football Playoff via X

Miami, Georgia, Utah and Indiana nabbed the top 4 spots in the first College Football Playoff rankings released last night, Axios' Donica Phifer writes.

  • Why it matters: The final of six weekly rankings will determine the bracket for the 12-team playoff.

UCLA — one of just three undefeated teams along with Miami and Utah — was ranked No. 8 because of a weak schedule.

  • Ohio State (6-2) is the first team out of the playoffs. If the regular season ended today, No. 25 Boise State would make it in as the best team from a non-major conference.
